title: COVID-19 and Gastrointestinal Symptoms
description: Dr. Carmen McDermott a physician from the Spokane Teaching Health Center, Sacred Heart Medical Center in Spokane, Washington and the University of Washington School of Medicine in Seattle, Washington, reviews her article appearing in the November 2020 issue of Mayo Clinic Proceedings where she notes that although previously underplayed as a sign or symptom of COVID-19, gastrointestinal symptoms do indeed emerge as presenting symptoms in the disease and can do so independently of respiratory symptoms.  She shares there is a potential link between fecal oral transmission and offers concrete steps patients and institutions can take to mitigate potential infection transmission. Available at: https://mayocl.in/2SfOjql

As well as practices like covering toilets. And patient care areas,. Could be important to helping prevent the transmission. In our article, we provide some specific instructions. And suggestions that hospitals. And healthcare facilities can take. Hello, my name is Carmen McDermott. I'm a faculty educator. With the Internal Medicine Residency Program. At Sacred Heart Medical Center and clinical instructor with University of Washington School. Of Medicine in Spokane, Washington. I co-authored the article, COVID-19 and Gastrointestinal Symptoms, Recognition, Containment, and Learning. From the Past. Our article discusses the gastrointestinal symptoms that clinicians need to be aware. Of in COVID-19, namely diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal discomfort. We discuss that patients can present with gastrointestinal symptoms and not have any. Respiratory symptoms. And we talk about the possibility of fecal-oral transmission and what hospitals and healthcare. Facilities can do to address the issue. The general public should understand that COVID-19 can start with gastrointestinal symptoms. Like nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. In addition to that, adherence to really excellent hand hygiene in public restrooms could be. A really important way of reducing virus transmission. There are still many questions remaining. We still need to understand whether fecal-oral spread is a major or minor route of transmission. For this virus. We need to understand the role of restrooms and whether flushing is an important aspect. That we need to be aware of. That's going to take some more research to sort out. We also need to understand how long people are contagious with the virus after they've. Had gastrointestinal symptoms. We need to look at perhaps toilet and ventilation design systems to see if those play a role. In either preventing or promoting transmission of the virus as well. So there's a lot of research. That we need to still do and a lot we don't quite understand yet. Thanks for listening to me discuss. Our article. In summary, we discuss the importance of looking at past coronavirus outbreaks to learn. About the gastrointestinal symptoms and possibility of fecal-oral transmission in this current. Outbreak. We discuss important aspects that clinicians and patients can be aware of and. Steps that healthcare facilities can take to address the issue. We hope you found this. annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it presents medical education about gastrointestinal symptoms that may occur with COVID-19 and identifies a related Mayo Clinic Proceedings article. Its discussion of possible fecal-oral transmission focuses on hygiene and healthcare-facility measures while acknowledging uncertainty about the route's importance. The publication and social-media links are presented as informational destinations, with no request for payment, credentials, investment, or other deceptive participation.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The main content explains clinical symptoms, discusses a possible transmission route with stated uncertainty, and offers healthcare-setting precautions.
